USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current posture and pursue a negotiating track while the Section 301 IP/technology-transfer investigation completes its 12-month statutory window and the Section 232 steel/aluminum decision is finalized. Do not preemptively impose broad China-specific tariffs now; instead use the pending investigations as leverage to seek substantive concessions on forced technology transfer and structural IP practices, keeping open the option of tariff action if Beijing continues to rebuff talks (as it did after consultations were declined). This avoids triggering a full trade war before the US has consolidated its evidentiary and political position.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests is modest and, on balance, tilts toward opportunity. As of 2018-03-01 the US has not yet levied China-specific tariffs — the only tariff action to date is the global Section 201 solar/washer safeguard (timeline, 2018-01-22), and the Section 301 investigation (initiated Aug 2017) remains open with its findings not yet issued, while Commerce only recommended steel/aluminum 232 remedies on Feb 16, 2018. China declined the Section 301 consultation request and voiced 'strong dissatisfaction,' yet made no structural concessions at the Nov 2017 Beijing visit. Meanwhile US macro health is solid: industrial production is rising (101.71 in Feb), consumer sentiment rebounded to 99.7 after a December dip, and the 10-year yield climbed to 2.87% on strong growth/inflation expectations — no material GDP drag or export-sector wound from the dispute yet. That combination (a pending investigation the US controls as leverage, no real-economy damage suffered, Chinese intransigence on IP) grounds a mild opportunity/leverage reading rather than a threat. The action stance is therefore mild: negotiate (action_score +0.1) without new commitments, letting the Section 301 and 232 processes apply the pressure rather than escalating tariff rhetoric prematurely — escalation now would risk immediate Chinese retaliation and a broader trade war before the US has cashed in its investigative leverage.
key_factors: Section 301 investigation still open with no findings or tariffs yet as of 2018-03-01
Only tariff action so far is global Section 201 solar/washer safeguard, not China-specific
Commerce recommended Section 232 steel/aluminum tariffs on Feb 16, 2018, decision pending
China declined consultation request and made no structural concessions at Nov 2017 Beijing visit
US economy robust: IP rising 101.71, consumer sentiment 99.7, 10Y at 2.87%

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Maintain a posture of active negotiation without new concessions — keep the Trump–Xi engagement channel open and signal willingness to address US commercial grievances, while holding firm on our core technology-sovereignty agenda (Made in China 2025) and preparing contingency responses in case Washington issues a punitive Section 301 finding. Do not escalate now: provoking a broader trade war with the US would hit our export economy far harder than it would hurt theirs, and no matching offer exists that would justify concession. Watch the imminent USTR announcement closely and calibrate response to its actual content.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is real and building but not yet material. The Section 301 investigation launched in August 2017 (per the timeline, 2017-08-14) directly targets China's technology-transfer and IP practices — the very foundation of our tech self-sufficiency push — and an affirmative finding with broad remedy recommendations was widely reported as imminent. This explains the moderate-high threat reading. However, as of this decision date no broad tariff, entity-list, or firm-level action (e.g. against Huawei) has been imposed: only narrow Section 201 safeguard tariffs on solar panels and washing machines are in effect (timeline 2018-01-22), and Section 232 steel/aluminium is still under investigation. The Chinese economy shows no sign of distress — January exports grew 11.1% in dollar terms and the yuan has strengthened ~9% over the year — so threat sits below the +0.5 'export sectors hit / firm targeting' anchor. This justifies an action stance in the negotiate band (0.0 to +0.1): escalating would hand Washington justification for the broad trade war it is clearly preparing for, while early concession would surrender leverage on technology-transfer rules with no US compromise to show for it. The right move is to manage the escalation phase diplomatically, keep the commercial-deal thread alive from the November 2017 Beijing visit, and avoid handing the US a pretext — while standing ready to retaliate defensively only if the US actually strikes.
key_factors: Section 301 investigation ongoing, targets China's tech-transfer/IP and Made in China 2025 — genuine strategic threat to tech autonomy
No broad tariff, entity-list, or firm-level action yet; only narrow Section 201 solar/washing-machine tariffs in effect
Section 232 steel/aluminium still under investigation, not yet actioned
China real economy solid: January exports +11.1% (dollar), yuan up ~9% over year — no material economic distress
Escalating now would hand Washington pretext for broader trade war; conceding now forfeits leverage with no US offer
Diplomatic channel open (Nov 2017 Beijing visit, commercial deals) — viable path to manage escalation
